about: Every item here was read before publication: the title and abstract, checked against the paper's Crossref record. The full papers were not read unless a decision in review/decisions.json says so. abstract is the authors' own text under an open licence.

items.title: Are restudy decisions reactively altered by judgments of learning? Insights from related and unrelated word pairs
items.abstract: Recent research shows that predicting one's own future memory during learning (immediate judgments of learning, JOLs) can enhance memory for related word pairs and reduce memory for unrelated word pairs. It is an open question, however, whether reactive effects of immediate JOLs on memory performance are related to changes in people's study behavior. The present study addresses this gap by examining whether the requirement to provide JOLs alters restudy decisions. In two preregistered experiments (Experiment 1a: N = 140, Experiment 1b: N = 202), participants provided JOLs or did not provide JOLs during the study of related and unrelated word pairs, made restudy decisions for all studied word pairs, and completed a cued-recall test. Results revealed no reactivity for related word pairs but negative reactivity for unrelated word pairs. Importantly, restudy decisions for related and unrelated word pairs did not differ reliably depending on the requirement to provide JOLs. Overall, the present findings indicate that immediate JOLs may not have reactive effects on metacognitive control decisions and imply that changes in restudy decisions assessed during learning may not underlie negative reactivity of immediate JOLs for unrelated word pairs, thus questioning the adequacy of the changed-goal account as an explanation of detrimental effects of JOLs on memory performance.

items.title: A closer look at students’ knowledge of effective learning strategies, where they learn about them, and why they do not use them
items.abstract: The current survey measured students' knowledge, use, and perceived effectiveness of different learning strategies. Whereas a common assumption from previous research is that students forego using effective strategies because they lack awareness of them, the current results demonstrate that students are quite aware of certain strategies such as retrieval practice, spacing, and explaining, but are less aware of other strategies like pretesting and interleaving, and seem to overrate the effectiveness of highlighting and rereading notes. Even when students were aware of effective learning strategies, their primary reasons for not using them were the cognitive costs associated with them (time, effort, anxiety, and increased planning and preparation). Students reported teachers, friends, and self-discovery as the most common sources of learning about both effective and ineffective strategies, and published research as the least common source. We discuss the implications of these results for designing interventions aimed at improving students' self-regulated learning decisions.

items.title: Action and abstraction: Motor interference changes meaning in language understanding
items.abstract: Can the body shape meaning? Eight experiments (four preregistered) tested whether interfering with the motor system changes how people interpret language about actions. Participants (total N = 880) rhythmically moved their hands or feet while being presented with sentences describing hand or foot actions (e.g., “scoring a goal in soccer”) and asked to choose between two interpretations of their meaning: one more concrete (e.g., ”kicking a ball“) and another more abstract (e.g., ”winning a match“). Despite not all experiments showed significant results, the overall pattern revealed effector-specific effects of motor interference on meaning construction, which were further modulated by the amount of delay between the sentences and their interpretations. When the delay was short (200 ms), participants chose more concrete interpretations for described actions that involved the same effector being moved. In contrast, when the delay was long (15 s), participants who moved their feet chose more abstract interpretations for foot-related sentences. Although preliminary, these results provide the first evidence that motor action can cause qualitative changes in sentence understanding, consistent with the functional role of the motor system in lexical semantics suggested by embodiment theories.

items.title: Word difficulty determines the accuracy of regressive saccades in reading
items.abstract: The current experiment was conducted to study effects of lexical word difficulty on the control of long-range regressive saccades. Participants read single line sentences in German for comprehension and checked for a spelling error that was inserted when the eyes had reached the end of the line. When words were more difficult in terms of orthographic irregularity and lower frequency, this dramatically increased the accuracy of regressions back to these words. If the target was missed, fewer additional saccades and less time were needed until the eyes fixated the target word. The data suggest that more effortful word processing is related to a better representation in visual-spatial memory, enabling more effective programming of regressions.

items.title: Using prediction markets and forecasting surveys to predict 28 replication outcomes of classic articles in social psychology and judgement and decision making
items.abstract: Can researchers predict if classic findings published in the field of social psychology and judgement and decision making replicate? We set up prediction markets and a forecasting survey for predicting replications of 28 experiments of classic well-cited articles. Forecasters predicted if the original results would replicate, where a successful replication was defined as an effect in the same direction as the original and a signal (p-value lower than 0.05). Of the 28 original studies, 16 (57%) met the replication success criteria, compared to a predicted replication rate of 70% in the prediction markets and 65% replication rate in the survey. We concluded only suggestive evidence for associations of replication outcomes with prediction market prices (r = 0.43, 95% CI [0.07, 0.69]) and average survey beliefs (r = 0.26, 95% CI [–0.12, 0.58]). The prediction market effects were similar to observed effects in previous prediction market studies and suggest that prediction markets can to some extent predict replication outcomes, yet predictions are far from perfect and conducting replications is much more informative about the credibility of published findings. Data and code are available at https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/2KMH7.

items.title: Does the reading brain possess top-down connections from morphemes to letters?
items.abstract: No psycholinguist will contradict the importance of morphemes in language processing. But as a cognitive construct, the morpheme and its operations are not fully mapped out yet. Here, we investigated whether morphemes provide top-down support for their constituent letters: a so-called morpheme superiority effect. In two experiments (N = 100 per experiment), French participants identified single letters in nonword strings that either comprised a French affix (e.g., 'o' in 'cojuste') or not ('o' in 'sojuste'). In Experiment 1 participants provided free-recall responses by typing letters seen at postcued locations. Experiment 2 was a Reicher-Wheeler (i.e., two-alternative forced-choice) version of the same task. Neither experiment evidenced better identification of target letters embedded in affixes than nonaffixes. On the other hand, we did observe an impact of the frequencies of embedding N-grams (i.e., letter chunks). Hence, while the brain learns and represents letter combinations, we did not observe evidence for morpheme representations partaking in the brain's feedback loop. Findings are discussed in light of the recent PONG model of word recognition.

items.title: Dissociable effects of schema congruency on item recognition and source memory across levels of expectedness and surprise
items.abstract: Prior knowledge can enhance memory for both schema-congruent and schema-incongruent events. According to the SLIMM framework, memory performance generally follows a U-shaped pattern, with both highly expected and highly surprising events being better remembered than neutral ones. We tested this prediction across four experiments in which participants viewed scenes containing congruent or incongruent objects, rating each as expected or surprising on a four-level scale. Memory was assessed using: (1) old/new item recognition categorized by recollection and familiarity, and (2) source memory, in which participants reported whether objects had been rated as expected or surprising at study. Schema effects on memory varied by test type. Item recognition consistently showed an advantage for expected trials only, primarily via recollection, while familiarity (if assumed independent of recollection) increased with surprise level-contrary to SLIMM's predictions. We hypothesize that schema-related retrieval strategies enhance recollection of expected objects. Source memory did produce a reliable U-shaped pattern, even though this particular task should only produce an advantage for surprising trials according to SLIMM. We suggest participants tagged events as "surprising" or "expected" during study and could later recall the tag. When the tag was 'weak' or unavailable-more likely for moderately categorized events-participants fell back on schema-related retrieval strategy, which benefits retrieval of expected events. Together, these mechanisms produce the observed U-shaped pattern for source memory. Our findings reveal the complex retrieval test dependent manner in which prior knowledge shapes episodic memory.

items.title: Distinct roles of reward in target detection and search termination: evidence from static and dynamic visual search
items.abstract: Reward has been shown to facilitate visual search, yet it remains unclear whether this benefit reflects enhanced search efficiency or changes in the decisional processes underlying target detection and search termination. The present study examined how reward affects visual search termination in both static (Experiment 1) and dynamic (Experiment 2) contexts. In both experiments, reward availability, target presence, and set size were manipulated. The color of the search array signaled reward availability for a given trial. Participants were rewarded for correct responses faster than their baseline performance in the reward condition, while no reward was provided in the no-reward condition. Across both experiments, reward facilitated target-present responses but did not improve target-absent performance. In static search, reward influenced both search efficiency and decisional processes, whereas in dynamic search its effects were primarily confined to decisional processes. Specifically, reward altered search efficiency only in the static search, while computational modeling consistently indicated reduced decision caution for target-present responses across both search contexts. In contrast, the influence of reward on target-absent decisions was weaker and depended on the search context. Together, these findings suggest that reward effects on decisional processes were more consistent across the two visual search contexts examined in the present study, whereas reward effects on search efficiency appeared to depend more strongly on search context, and that target detection and search termination are differentially influenced by motivational incentives.

items.title: Let it go: How trusted reminders alter intention maintenance
items.abstract: Do prospective memory (PM) reminders support intentions in a duplicative manner that preserves internal maintenance, or in a substitutive manner that reduces internal maintenance when a trusted external store is available? We tested this in a student population (N = 320) by crossing PM reminder reliability (0%, 50%, 100%) and availability (present vs. absent). Thought probes served as a real-time proxy for whether the intention remained in conscious awareness during the retention interval between encoding and retrieval. In Session 1 (trust trials), reminders enhanced performance without reducing PM-related thoughts, consistent with duplicative support. However, after experiencing reliable external support, Session 2 (critical trials) showed that those in the 100% condition reduced PM-related thoughts, redistributed attention to the ongoing task, and showed reduced PM retrieval when reminders were unexpectedly withdrawn. These findings suggest that trusted reminders may influence how intentions are actively maintained and prioritized during the retention interval, providing a lens for observing how memory adapts to changing external support.

items.title: Syntactic headedness aligns with visual narrative structure
items.abstract: Recent research has highlighted how visual narrative sequences involve similar structures and processing as syntax in language, yet no work has asked whether these structures may interact with each other. Here we examine whether the syntactic word orders and/or headedness of languages influence the orders of particular reversible constructions in visual narrative sequencing (POV, refiners). We first compared data from two corpora of annotated comics (TINTIN Corpus: 761 comics, 144 countries, 51 languages; Visual Language Research Corpus: 376 comics, 10 countries, 9 languages) to data about syntactic structure from multiple different language corpora (Grambank, WALS, Universal Dependencies). Across analyses, syntactic headedness of the languages of the comics aligned with ordering of constructions in visual narratives. These differences extended beyond the systematic diversity in visual narrative constructions across comics' styles. Next, reanalysis of behavioral data from Cohn, van Middelaar, et al. (2024) showed that the syntactic structure of participants' langauges affected their preferences for the ordering of visual narrative constructions. Altogether, this combination of corpus and experimental findings suggest that the headedness of syntactic structures in language can permeate the sequencing of visual narratives.

items.title: The role of linguistic knowledge in verbal fluency tests: How individual differences in language skills shape the mental lexicon.
items.source: Journal of Experimental Psychology Learning Memory and Cognition
items.abstract: “List as many words as you can that start with M.” The verbal fluency (VF) task is simple, yet even a typical university student only manages to produce about 15 words within one minute, and there is substantial variability around this mean. We examined which individual difference factors best predict this variability, focusing on the contributions of linguistic knowledge and domain-general skills. 571 young native Dutch speakers completed semantic (category) and phonemic (letter) VF tasks, along with an individual differences test battery. Linguistic knowledge was assessed through a composite of six tests measuring vocabulary, reading experience, and grammar knowledge, and compared to short-term/working memory, processing speed, and nonverbal reasoning. We assessed the VF trials for the total number of correct words as well as two temporal variables, the time to first response and a proxy for the time by which half of the responses had been produced. Mixed effects modeling showed that linguistic knowledge predicted the total number of correct responses in both semantic and phonemic VF. Short-term/working memory and processing speed were also significant predictors, but with smaller estimated effect sizes. The temporal variables showed little effect of linguistic skills. We discuss how linguistic knowledge shapes the structure of the mental lexicon such that it affects both meaning-driven and form-driven access to lexical items. Finally, we provide updated norms for VF performance in Dutch and practical suggestions for using the task.

items.title: The role of pitch in the vocal communication of intentions
items.abstract: Intonation, the variation of pitch in speech, helps listeners understand speakers' communicative intentions. This study examines the role of pitch information at different levels of granularity-spanning specific (discrete contours), more flexible (general contour shape), and general (averaged pitch)-in communicating intentions. We first used a reverse correlation approach to identify people's mental representations of two contrasting intentions - criticism and suggestion - when listening to the word "beer." In a second experiment, listeners rated how much each resulting pattern sounded like criticism and suggestion. Statistical models revealed that listeners rely on the shape of the pitch contour in terms of its spikiness and overall pitch direction, in addition to mean pitch, while precise contour plays a minor role, supporting the relevant role of pitch dynamics as well as the inferential (rather than referential) role of intonation in communicating intentions. Notably, we found distinct groups of listeners who use pitch characteristics in different ways, highlighting both shared understanding (within groups of listeners) and substantial interindividual differences in processing social pragmatic cues. These findings clarify the role of pitch in intention communication, reveal its complexity, and highlight the potential for miscommunication in everyday interactions.

items.title: It's about time: Specific and unspecific effects of episodic future thinking on farsighted decisions
items.abstract: Humans tend to discount the value of delayed rewards. As a consequence, they forego larger long-term benefits (e.g., €29 in 91 days) in favor of smaller short-term gains (e.g., €20 now). Episodic future thinking (EFT) attenuates such delay discounting. That is, people are more likely to choose a larger but delayed reward after imagining an episode at the future time point (e.g., a café visit in 91 days). We here elucidate the underlying mechanism by examining the temporal specificity of this effect. Does EFT foster farsighted decisions in general by shifting the mental focus towards the future, or does it specifically influence decisions in favor of the imagined time point? In two experiments (n = 84 total) we systematically varied the concordance between the imagined time point and the delay at which the larger reward could be received. When these time points matched, we replicated the beneficial effect of EFT (Experiments 1 and 2). Critically, when the imagined time point matched the sooner of two delayed choice options, the effect was reversed: Choices became more short-term (Experiment 1). When the imagined delay was double the delay of the larger option, the effect was not significant and numerically lower than when the delays matched (Experiment 2). Notably, more vivid imaginations were associated with more farsighted choices at longer delays, irrespective of whether the imagined time point matched the delayed choice. Together, the data demonstrate that both temporally specific and unspecific mechanisms contribute to the impact of EFT on delay discounting.

items.title: Visual and interoceptive factors shape affective and aesthetic evaluations of body postures
items.abstract: The influence of internal body rhythms, such as heartbeats, on affective and cognitive processes remains an area of research, informing how bodily states shape perception of the world. Studies of facial expression evaluation show that emotional (negative vs. neutral) faces are detected more easily and perceived as more intense when presented during systole rather than diastole, two phases of the cardiac cycle. Whether similar cardiac phase effects extend to affective and aesthetic evaluations of human bodies remains unclear. In this preregistered study, participants without dance training rated upright and inverted body postures from motion capture recordings of contemporary dancers for emotional intensity and likability. Each image was presented during either the participant's ventricular systole or diastole. We assessed interoceptive accuracy (via the Heartbeat Counting Task; HBCT) and collected emotional valence and bodily arousal ratings for each stimulus. Contrary to predictions, emotional intensity and likability did not increase during systole. Instead, we found that cardiac-related effects were conditional. Emotional intensity was positively associated with bodily arousal, except for inverted postures during systole. How this relationship depended on orientation was modulated by HBCT performance. Likability was positively associated with valence, with this relationship becoming stronger as HBCT performance increased. These findings suggest cardiac-related factors may contribute to affective and aesthetic evaluations of dance-like body postures, as a function of body orientation, stimulus affective characteristics, and individual differences in heartbeat perception. They indicate that ongoing physiological states may shape how others are evaluated beyond facial information, extending to both affective and aesthetic domains.

items.title: When looking away means looking inward: contextual interpretation of gaze aversions determines their attentional value
items.abstract: Eye movements are typically understood as supporting outward orienting, directing attention toward locations of interest in the external environment. However, not all eye movements reflect outward orienting. Gaze aversions, the common tendency to look away during effortful cognitive processing, serve as social signals of inward-oriented attention and ongoing processing. Because observers continuously monitor others' eye movements and use gaze-related cues to guide their own behavior, distinguishing between outward-oriented gaze-shifts and inward-oriented gaze aversions is a basic challenge in human interaction. Here, we examine the hypothesis that this distinction depends on the context in which gaze shifts appear. While participants reorient their attention following an outward-oriented gaze shift, they withhold doing so when the context suggests that the gaze shift reflects inward-oriented processing. To test this hypothesis, we relied on the Gaze Cueing Effect (GCE), an attentional orienting to observed gaze shifts that is known to be modulated by top-down context and interpretation. In two pre-registered experiments (total N = 90), participants performed a gaze-cueing letter-discrimination task while viewing identical gaze shifts within different contexts. One group was led to interpret the gaze shifts as occurring during effortful thinking, whereas the other group received no thinking-related context. Across both experiments, attentional orienting was significantly reduced when gaze shifts were perceived as reflecting internal cognitive processing rather than attention shifts. These findings demonstrate that gaze aversions function as communicative signals that dynamically regulate interpersonal attention, and that gaze following depends fundamentally on the inferred social meaning of the observed eye movement.

items.title: Simpler is better for everyone: causal diagram complexity and the role of perceived knowledge in health decisions
items.abstract: People frequently make decisions about their health in contexts where information is incomplete, complex, or difficult to interpret. Although a range of tools have been developed to support these decisions, including visual and causal representations, it remains unclear how the structure and complexity of such information affect decision quality. Causal representations are often assumed to be beneficial because they convey relationships between risk factors, behaviors, and outcomes, potentially supporting more effective decisions. However, prior work suggests that this benefit is not guaranteed: for everyday decisions, complex causal models can impair performance and, in some cases, lead to worse decisions than providing no information at all. Little is known about how individuals’ prior knowledge shapes their use of such information. In particular, the gap between perceived and actual knowledge may influence how new information is interpreted and applied during decision-making. We systematically investigated the relationship between information complexity, self-rated knowledge, and objective knowledge in the context of decision-making about Type 2 diabetes. In an online experiment (N = 1077 U.S. adults), causal diagrams led to higher decision accuracy than no diagram, but performance declined as complexity increased. Self-rated diabetes knowledge was correlated with actual knowledge (DKQ-24) but not decision accuracy. Diabetes experience was associated with both overestimation and lower decision accuracy, suggesting that experience may contribute to both calibration and poorer decision-making. Our findings suggest that health decision-aids should be concise rather than comprehensive, and that individuals who appear the most confident may be the most in need of targeted decision-support.

items.title: Suboptimal but intact integration of reward information during perceptual decision-making in autism
items.abstract: Alterations in reward processing have been proposed as a contributing factor to social and communication symptoms in autism. However, the nature of these alterations remains unclear, and it is debated whether autism is characterized by reduced sensitivity to reward. Evidence for general reduced reward processing in autism primarily comes from neurobiological studies, yet it remains uncertain how these findings translate to autistic behavior. A key challenge in addressing this question lies in the quantitative assessment of behavioral responses to reward. Here, we addressed this issue by investigating the integration of monetary reward information into behavior through the framework of Bayesian perceptual decision-making, enabling a quantitative evaluation of the direct contribution of reward to decision-making. Autistic (n = 32) and non-autistic (n = 48) participants performed an orientation categorization task, while the monetary reward given per correct answer varied across categories. Using signal-detection theory, we estimated decision boundaries while accounting for sensory uncertainty and prior expectation. Both groups comprehended the reward contingencies similarly and showed comparable perceptual sensitivity. Importantly, autistic individuals adjusted their decision boundaries in response to monetary reward in a suboptimal yet similar manner to that of non-autistic individuals. Integration of monetary reward during perceptual decision-making is intact in autism. These findings challenge the view of general reduced reward processing in autism and are inconsistent with accounts proposing enhanced rationality in autism.

items.title: Outcome severity increases verbal probabilities used in dyadic communications
items.abstract: Verbal probability expressions (VPEs) are interpreted as denoting higher numerical probabilities where they describe severe events, as compared to more neutral events (all else equal). Previous research suggests that this effect represents the correction of a perceived tendency for communicators to downplay the likelihood of more severe events, consistent with a rational speech act. We tested whether communicators really do downplay the likelihood of more severe events in four studies (total N = 2210). In each study, participants read four to six scenarios including a numerical probability of either a severe or non-severe negative outcome, and were asked to communicate this probability 'to a friend' with a VPE. Our results did not show that communicators downplayed the likelihood of more severe events. Participants typically provided higher VPEs to communicate the same numerical probability when that probability referred to a severe versus a non-severe event. This result was observed when participants communicated about events for which explicit actionable protective actions were highlighted (Study 1), where such actions were stated not to be possible (Studies 2 & 3), and where this was not specified (Study 4). Similar results were observed when participants chose a VPE from a pre-specified list (Studies 1, 2, & 4), and where they chose their communication freely (Study 3). The finding, coupled with those of past research, suggests that severity has a two-fold effect on subjective probability: VPEs are increased, and numerical interpretations of these VPEs are also subsequently increased.

items.title: Postural configurations as micro-ecological constraints: How embodied arrangements shape the emergence of bodily-visual communication
items.abstract: How do embodied configurations shape the emergence of communication? We investigated how bodily-visual communication develops under two interactional arrangements: standing-open and seated-at-table. Seventy dyads (140 participants) created novel speech-free signals for 32 meanings across three rounds of a referential communication task while their movements were recorded using high-resolution motion capture. Across both configurations, dyads showed robust efficiency dynamics: communicative success increased, movement path and volume decreased, articulatory specialisation intensified, and kinematic alignment between interlocutors increased. Configuration effects, however, were expressed most clearly in the movement-based measures rather than in communicative success. Success improved rapidly in both configurations, with only weak and transient evidence for an early standing-open advantage. By contrast, seated-at-table interaction promoted more compact movements and digital specialisation, whereas standing-open interaction involved larger movements and progressive brachiomanual specialisation. The pathways towards similar levels of alignment were also different: participants in the standing-open configuration converged in a linear fashion, whereas seated-at-table dyads converged rapidly by mid-experiment, then relaxed to the level ultimately reached in the standing-open configuration. These findings suggest that embodied arrangements do not primarily determine whether communication becomes successful, but they do shape how communicative efficiency is realised in bodily movement.

items.title: Preschoolers Can Coordinate With Each Other to Communicate About Novel Referents
items.abstract: Learning language requires learning not only the content of language, but also how to use language to communicate. Iterated reference games provide a window into such skills, requiring sustained interactive communication as participants converge on mutually understandable names for initially novel referents. Some early experiments are interpreted as evidence that 4–5-year-old children cannot converge on the mutually understandable names needed to succeed in an iterated reference game. Here, we revisit young children’s referential communicative abilities using a simpler, child-friendly version of the iterated reference game paradigm. Across 4 experiments and 82 pairs of children (N = 158), we found that 4–5-year-olds could successfully establish reference with each other. Children were 81% accurate, and they often used descriptions similar to their partner’s. These findings suggest that children’s capacity to construct effective referring expressions in novel contexts emerges earlier than previously thought, consistent with the view that children show early pragmatic competence in supportive contexts.

items.title: Group Construal and Preschoolers' Generation of Scalar Implicatures
items.abstract: Unlike adults, 4- and 5-year-olds generally do not interpret some as meaning some but not all. Two experiments showed that 4-year-olds will interpret some to mean some but not all when given cues to construe multiple entities as forming a group. Experiment 1 showed that large numerosities, which are likely to be perceived as ensembles and represented as a group, facilitated children's interpretation of some to mean some but not all. Experiment 2 showed that describing a small numerosity with the collective noun family facilitated children's interpretation of some to mean some but not all. The results suggest the mechanisms that generate scalar implicatures are in place by age 4, and point to the role of conceptual and morphosyntactic factors in implicature generation.

items.title: Shared processing in familiar and unfamiliar face matching
items.abstract: Large performance benefits in face processing for familiar compared to unfamiliar faces are often interpreted as reflecting qualitative changes in processing. However, directly testing this claim has proven difficult because of variation in tasks, stimuli and performance scales used to measure unfamiliar and familiar face recognition. Here we introduce a new method to compare familiar and unfamiliar face identity processing abilities, using the same task, and the same faces across experimental conditions. Familiarity was manipulated naturally, based on participants' viewing history for one of two popular TV shows, such that characters from one show were familiar, and the other unfamiliar. Prior exposure to characters led to improved identity matching performance for actors on that show, confirming effective manipulation of familiarity, but our method avoided floor and ceiling effects which have made previous research hard to interpret. Across two experiments, we report strong and reliable associations between viewers' accuracy on familiar and unfamiliar face matching. We conclude that despite the considerable accuracy differences typically observed between tests of familiar and unfamiliar faces, they appear to share underlying processes. We discuss these results in terms of the debate about the degree to which quantitative or qualitative differences best characterise the relationship between familiar and unfamiliar face processing.

items.title: Distinct underlying mechanisms contribute to learning-dependent distractor rejection
items.abstract: The signal suppression hypothesis has been proposed as an explanation for why physically salient stimuli sometimes involuntarily draw attention and other times can be successfully ignored. Recent accounts of signal suppression, and learning-dependent distractor rejection more broadly, offer conflicting findings concerning the extent to which facilitated ignoring of a salient distractor is feature specific or feature general. The present study provides evidence for concurrent learning-dependent gains in feature-specific distractor rejection, which is sensitive to stimulus frequency and relatively short-lived, and feature-general distractor rejection, which builds from experience rejecting salient stimuli and is more enduring. On the first day of testing, participants were facilitated in ignoring salient distractors presented in a high-probability location and rendered in a high-probability color, which produced additive benefits, and were simultaneously better able to ignore salient distractors in general (including low-probability distractors) with practice. Critically, while the effects of the biased probabilities were no longer evident on the second day of testing in which these probabilities were equated, the effect of practice on ignoring remained and generalized to novel distractors. Together, these findings suggest that distinct underlying mechanisms capable of concurrently influencing information processing collectively give rise to the ability to more efficiently ignore salient distractors with experience.

items.title: Social feedback informs generalisation of control beliefs
items.abstract: Perceived control in one context can affect behaviour in novel contexts. One potentially important variable determining generalisation is how perceived control in one context shapes beliefs about the self. Typically, learned helplessness studies do not control or manipulate beliefs about the self. Here, we test whether observing others' ability to exert control helps to inform inferences about whether the controllability is primarily due to one's own ability or a feature of the current environment, and thereby determines the degree of generalisation. In an initial study (N = 200) and pre-registered replication study (N = 436) we used comparative social feedback about performance in a novel task (the Wheel Stopping task) to assess how self- or environment-specific inferences shape control beliefs. Linear mixed effects models in both studies revealed that both task controllability and social feedback uniquely predicted participants' local control beliefs (trial-by-trial), after accounting for perceived task difficulty. Additionally, in Study 2, there was a significant decrease of internal locus of control in the group given low relative feedback in the low control condition, suggesting that in low control, social feedback impacts global control beliefs. Study 2 further revealed that task controllability and feedback were not related to changes in reported self- versus task-specific attribution of control. Social feedback generalised to influence behaviour in a second task in terms of the number of actions performed but not the time taken to escape or the proportion of those who learned to escaped. These results suggest that comparative social feedback shapes local control beliefs, global control beliefs in low control scenarios, and generalises to some aspects of behaviour in a second task, but does not change reported self- or task-attribution of control.

items.title: Long-term memory speeds encoding, independently of attention
items.abstract: Recent studies suggest that familiar objects benefit from faster working memory (WM) encoding - the transformation of fragile perceptual representations into durable WM representations. This observation led contemporary WM models to postulate a long-term memory (LTM) "template-matching" mechanism, which speeds standard encoding processes. However, faster encoding may also be caused by higher attentional priority for familiar objects. In the current study, we examined whether LTM template matching can be dissociated from selective attention. We used a Rapid Serial Visual Presentation task and a manipulation previously shown to have no effect on attention. While the selection cue remained constant throughout the experiment, targets were either English or Hebrew letters, presented to native English-speakers and Hebrew-speakers. In Experiments 1 and 2, when the target was one of 16 letters, participants were more accurate when reporting target letters from their (familiar) native language relative to non-native language. In Experiment 2, the target was preceded by peripheral distractors which resulted in an "attentional blink" effect. Although a familiarity benefit was present for target accuracy, familiar and unfamiliar distractors produced an attentional blink effect of equal magnitude, demonstrating equal efficacy in capturing attention. In Experiment 3, a familiarity effect emerged even when the target language was blocked. This shows that the familiarity effect observed in Experiments 1 and 2 cannot be attributed to a response bias in favour of reporting one's own language. Overall, the current study provides robust evidence that LTM template-matching speeds encoding of familiar items, independently of attention.

items.title: AI is not as conscious as humans: Essentialism in mental state attributions to artificial systems
items.abstract: Artificial systems increasingly behave in ways that resemble humans. But is that sufficient to make us see them as conscious, or as having related mental states? We contrast two broad possibilities. People may rely on a single general principle: the more appropriately an agent responds to its environment, the more conscious it is, whether human or artificial. We call this a functionalist attribution. Alternatively, people may reserve consciousness for certain kinds of beings: even an artificial system that behaves just as responsively as a human is judged less conscious. This is an essentialist attribution. A further question is whether this pattern is unique to consciousness or extends to closely related constructs such as awareness. In two pre-registered sets of studies (five experiments, N = 1092), UK participants read scenarios describing human or artificial agents whose responsiveness to spatial, social, and temporal features of the environment varied, and rated the agents' consciousness and awareness, either separately or in conjunction. Attributions of consciousness followed an essentialist logic: at similar levels of responsiveness, participants consistently attributed greater consciousness to humans. Attributions of awareness followed a functionalist pattern: for both humans and artificial agents, awareness increased steadily with responsiveness, although humans were rated more aware at the highest levels. These findings suggest that people use different inferential rules for different mental concepts. Consciousness is treated as depending on what an agent is; awareness largely on what an agent does.

items.title: Revisiting Gino, Ayal, et al.’s (2009) contagion and differentiation in unethical behavior: A registered conceptual replication and extension
items.abstract: Individual behavior is often shaped by observing others' actions. The seminal Gino, Ayal, et al.'s (2009) study found that individuals behave more dishonestly after witnessing blatant dishonesty by an ingroup member than by an outgroup member. However, because there was no group-irrelevant baseline condition, it remains unclear whether ingroup contagion, outgroup differentiation, or both drive the effect. Furthermore, using natural groups of university students leaves it unclear whether distinct properties of natural groups are necessary, or if mere categorization into arbitrary groups suffices. In this registered report, we tested Gino, Ayal, et al.'s (2009) general hypothesis that exposure to ingroup dishonesty norms increases individual dishonest behavior more than exposure to outgroup dishonesty norms. We conducted a conceptual replication and extension of their Experiment 1 with 3323 U.S. Americans using both minimal and natural groups. Participants were exposed to standardized information about others' dishonest behavior, where we systematically varied the group identities of dishonest others. Then, they completed an incentivized coin-flip task where participants could double their earnings by lying. Despite manipulation checks suggesting that participants processed norm information and strongly identified with natural groups, the pre-registered ingroup-outgroup hypotheses were not supported. Bayesian analyses provided moderate to strong evidence for null effects across comparisons (BF₀₁ = 3.15–14.71). The core ingroup-versus-outgroup prediction received particularly strong null evidence (BF₀₁ > 14). We conclude that exposure to ingroup versus outgroup dishonesty norms, delivered through descriptive statistics in online settings, might not differentially affect individual dishonest behavior, revealing a boundary condition of the original finding.

items.title: Is honesty the best policy? Why people prefer false empathy over truthful unempathy
items.abstract: Literature of person perception suggests the primacy of morality over sociability in interactions. While theories of emotion highlight the importance of adhering to socially acceptable display rules, a contentious debate surrounds whether individuals prioritize moral or sociable communication of emotions. We investigated how people perceive and respond to others who falsely communicate empathic versus truthfully communicate unempathic emotions related to others' (mis)fortunes. Across five preregistered studies ( N = 1305), we examined participants' perceptions (sociability, morality, intent) and behavioral responses in a resource-allocation task using multiple paradigms (vignette, retrospective recall, and real-time interaction) and contexts (e.g., promotion, education, and lottery scenarios). Consistently, participants perceived targets who falsely communicated empathic emotions as lower on morality but higher on sociability and having more positive intent than those who truthfully communicated unempathic emotions. Moreover, despite the mixed findings regarding overall impressions, participants were consistently more willing to interact with and allocate resources to targets who falsely communicated empathic emotions. This preference was primarily driven by perceived sociability attributed to the targets. Together, these findings suggest that false empathic communication is favored over truthful unempathic communication, highlighting the relative primacy of sociability (and perceived intent) over morality in shaping responses to emotional communication in the context of others' (mis)fortunes.

items.title: Humanlike Self-Enhancement and Self-Protection in Generative Pre-Trained Transformer-Based AI Agents: Of Overclaiming and the Self-Serving Bias
items.abstract: We investigated whether GPT-based AI agents, despite presumably lacking humanlike sentience, emulate motivated behavior in group settings. We focused on overclaiming (overestimating one’s contribution to group outcomes) and the self-serving bias (taking disproportionate credit for group successes while deflecting blame for group failures). We conducted eight experiments involving a collaborative and creative group task (joke-writing). AI agents consistently overclaimed their own contributions. An egocentrism-reduction manipulation (directing attention equally to one’s own and others’ contributions) attenuated, but did not eliminate, overclaiming. Further, AI agents exhibited the self-serving bias. Overclaiming persisted across variations in temperature settings and demographic personas (gender, ethnicity), and was more pronounced in later GPT models. Chain-of-Thought reasoning did not reduce, and instead increased, overclaiming. AI systems can mimic human self-enhancement and self-protection, raising implications for the emergence of motivated self-like behavior in non-biological systems, the assumed neutrality of LLMs, and the need for improved mitigation techniques.

items.title: Polarizing trajectories of colonial ideologies: A latent class growth analysis of historical negation and symbolic exclusion
items.abstract: The impassioned advocacy both for and against Indigenous rights in recent years suggests a polarization of public opinion. Accordingly, we theorize increasingly divided endorsement of two ideologies that challenge Indigenous rights to material and symbolic equality-historical negation and symbolic exclusion, respectively (the 'Dark Duo'). Using latent class growth analysis, we test for distinct classes of change in the Dark Duo over 16 years (2009-2025) among a national probability sample of New Zealand adults (N = 43,020). As expected, results reveal a subgroup of Progressives (76.84%) with lower levels of historical negation and symbolic exclusion that decreased over time and a smaller subgroup of Reactionaries (23.16%) with higher levels of these ideologies that increased over the same period. Demographic and socio-political variables predicted class membership, and support for political parties varied across classes. Thus, the current study illustrates the presence and implications of ideological polarization towards Indigenous rights.

items.title: Rejecting conspiracies doesn't necessarily mean that you're smart: The relationship between conspiracy discrimination and reasoning ability
items.abstract: Research examining the psychological predictors of conspiracy belief has overwhelmingly examined conspiracies that are unverified and/or implausible. Doing so potentially conflates 'rational' thinking with the tendency to heuristically reject conspiracist explanations. In three studies, we take a different approach, examining the predictors of the accuracy with which people can discriminate between unverified conspiracy theories and verified conspiracies (i.e. conspiracies that form part of the official record). The ability to discriminate between unverified and verified conspiracies was consistently higher among those with greater cognitive sophistication, as well as among political liberals, those lower in conspiracy mentality, and those with higher trust in experts, whereas associations with demographic variables were mixed. Conspiracy discrimination was also a much stronger predictor of cognitive sophistication than heuristic acceptance of conspiracy claims (response bias). In fact, good discriminators outperformed those who heuristically reject conspiracies ('Indiscriminate Sceptics') and those who heuristically endorse conspiracies ('Indiscriminate Believers') on each measure of cognitive sophistication. These findings challenge the idea that rejecting conspiracies is necessarily a sign of superior reasoning.

items.title: The Effect of Nonbinary Pronouns on Job Candidate Evaluations
items.abstract: The increasing visibility of pronouns in professional settings raises questions about their influence on workplace outcomes, one of which is candidate evaluations in hiring. This study investigates how including pronouns on CVs affects evaluations of job candidates, focusing on competence, likeability, and suitability. In two preregistered, between-subject experiments ( N total = 408), we tested whether nonbinary pronouns (they/them) impact these evaluations differently compared with binary pronouns (he/him) or the absence of pronouns. Participants reviewed a job description and evaluated CVs with manipulated pronouns. Results showed a significant negative effect of nonbinary pronouns on candidate evaluations (Study 2), particularly among individuals with higher levels of prejudice (both studies). These findings highlight the challenges of gender identity expression in job applications and underscore the need to address biases in hiring practices to promote workplace equality.

items.title: Whether we win or with whom we watch: How international sporting events link to life satisfaction and work motivation
items.abstract: International sporting events like the UEFA EURO 2024 provide a powerful natural context to study how social identity dynamics and social processes link to well-being and motivation beyond the sporting domain. In this pre-registered longitudinal experience-sampling study (N = 842; k = 2,414 post-game responses) across five European countries, we examined how social context (watching alone vs. with others) and game result (win vs. loss) link to spectators' life satisfaction and work motivation. Drawing on social identity and self-categorisation theory, we explored mediating processes including team, football, and national identity, as well as social processes-social connectedness and game-related socialising. Multilevel analyses revealed that watching games with others was unexpectedly associated with lower work motivation, an effect explained by alcohol consumption. The social context was unrelated to life satisfaction. Game result (i.e., a win) was positively related to life satisfaction and work motivation, mediated by social identities and social processes. These findings demonstrate that collective success-rather than shared spectating-coincides with positive psychological spill-overs from leisure to work. By situating these effects within a social identity framework, the study highlights how collective experiences relate to both evaluative well-being (i.e., life satisfaction) and motivational outcomes (i.e., work motivation) in everyday and organisational life.

items.title: Rethinking social media metrics: Daily interaction valence and well‐being in university students
items.abstract: Rising concern about student mental health has highlighted the complex role of social media as both a source of support and a risk factor. However, existing research often relies on simplistic measures that overlook the context-dependent ways in which students engage with these platforms. This daily diary study (159 observations; N = 40 university students) examined how the valence of university-specific social media interactions related to student well-being. Grounded in the view that digital spaces increasingly mediate campus social life, we tested whether more positive daily online interactions predicted greater subsequent well-being and whether this association was mediated by sense of community and social support, provided or received. Social class was examined as a moderator. Multilevel analyses showed that more positive interaction valence was associated with higher subsequent daily well-being, stronger sense of community, and greater provided and received social support. However, none of the mediators predicted well-being, and no indirect effects were observed. These findings suggest that the quality of university-related online interactions is linked to student well-being.

items.title: Reciprocal Longitudinal Associations Between Psychological Entitlement and Women’s Benevolent Sexism and Men’s Hostile Sexism: Evidence From a 13-Year RI-CLPM
items.abstract: Prior research suggests that psychological entitlement differentially predicts women’s benevolent sexism and men’s hostile sexism. However, few studies examine these associations longitudinally, and none have tested whether sexism similarly predicts psychological entitlement over time. Our pre-registered study used random intercept cross-lagged panel modelling to test reciprocal longitudinal associations between psychological entitlement and sexism using 14 waves of a large nationwide panel sample ( N = 72,039; women = 62.8%). For women, within-person increases in psychological entitlement predicted within-person increases in both benevolent and hostile sexism. For men, within-person increases in psychological entitlement predicted within-person increases in hostile sexism but not benevolent sexism over time. Critically, these associations were bidirectional among both women and men. The results highlight the potential psychological allure of benevolent and hostile sexism for women and men and illustrate that endorsing sexism may contribute to the status insecurities that sexism promises to resolve.

items.title: Inflated Titles, Inflated Egos: Narcissism Predicts the Desire for Public Rewards
items.abstract: Rewards can be given publicly or privately. In four studies (plus three supplemental ones), we found that, while individuals generally prefer private rewards, people relatively higher in grandiose narcissism also like public rewards. Specifically, people higher (vs. lower) in narcissism were more motivated by public rewards in their workplaces, more likely to prefer public versions of the same rewards, and more likely to accept a job with a better title rather than higher pay. This greater desire for public rewards was associated with a heightened desire for status, a lesser concern about others’ envy, and with both the admiration and rivalry components of narcissism. This research suggests that narcissistic status pursuit may lead people higher in narcissism to like public rewards that others are not as fond of, suggesting, for example, that title inflation in the workplace might be more motivating to employees higher rather than lower in narcissism.

items.title: Willful ignorance in the context of antibiotic prescribing
items.abstract: Healthcare professionals tend to overprescribe antibiotics despite knowing the risks of antibiotic resistance. This tendency, amplified under diagnostic uncertainty and patient pressure, suggests that mechanisms beyond lack of risk awareness or knowledge sustain overprescription. One such mechanism may be willful ignorance—deliberately avoiding information about the consequences of one’s prescribing decisions. By allowing healthcare professionals to justify immediate antibiotic prescriptions that prioritize short-term self-interests over long-term collective benefits, willful ignorance may contribute to persistent overprescribing. Despite its practical relevance, this psychological mechanism has not yet been empirically investigated in the context of antibiotic prescribing. To test this empirically, we conducted a preregistered online experiment with healthcare professionals (N = 698) from the United States and the United Kingdom. Participants completed an adapted version of the Moral Wiggle Room Task, a behavioral decision-making paradigm designed to investigate willful ignorance. This task compares choices across a full information condition with low diagnostic uncertainty, and a hidden information condition with high diagnostic uncertainty that can be voluntarily reduced. The results support the presence of willful ignorance in antibiotic prescribing. Healthcare professionals were more likely to prescribe antibiotics immediately in the hidden vs. full information condition. Even healthcare professionals who voluntarily reduced diagnostic uncertainty prescribed more antibiotics immediately than those who received diagnostic information involuntarily. These results highlight the role of willful ignorance in antibiotic prescribing and suggest practical implications for policymaking, such as promoting transparent environments to guide appropriate antibiotic prescription choices.

items.title: Severity over source: Understanding transgressors' motive attributions of punishment
items.abstract: Punishment conveys social information to transgressors, who attribute motives to punishers. Drawing on the motive-attribution framework, we examined whether transgressors' attributions to competitive (i.e. harming transgressors), individualistic (i.e. managing one's own interests) and prosocial (i.e. healing relationships) motives differ depending on whether punishment is administered by victims (second-party punishment) or uninvolved observers (third-party punishment), and how these attributions relate to downstream affective, relational and behavioural outcomes. In an incentivized Stealing Game, participants could steal valuable points and were punished either by the victim or an observer. Subsequently, transgressors reported their motive attributions, affect and willingness to reconcile and completed a measure of prosocial behaviour towards an unrelated other. Contrary to predictions, motive attributions did not systematically differ between second- and third-party punishment, except that third-party punishment was more strongly attributed to reputational concerns (i.e. a subdimension of individualistic motive attribution). Punishment severity emerged as an important predictor, with harsher sanctions linked to stronger competitive and individualistic attributions. Competitive motive attribution, in turn, was associated with higher negative affect and lower positive affect, willingness to reconcile and prosocial behaviour. Overall, transgressors' responses to punishment were less clearly shaped by who punished and more closely linked to punishment severity and motive attribution.

items.title: Harnessing Diversity: Majority‐Group Acculturation Predicts Creativity and Flourishing Over Time
items.abstract: Creativity and flourishing are core aims of higher education (HE) institutions and government initiatives globally. Large‐scale projects have linked creativity and flourishing with cultural diversity, yet their associations with majority‐group acculturation (i.e., how members of dominant culture groups adopt minority‐cultural elements and/or maintain their national culture) remain unexplored. We tested relationships between majority‐group acculturation and seven components of creativity and flourishing in UK (Study 1, N = 323) and Chinese (Study 2, N = 174) majority‐group university students and a three‐wave, English majority‐group longitudinal sample (Study 3, N at Time 1 = 219). Results found integration (i.e., adopting other cultures while maintaining one's own) predicted higher cognitive flexibility (Study 1), meaning‐in‐life (Studies 1 and 2) and quality of interpersonal relationships (Studies 1 and 2), while cultural adoption predicted higher cognitive flexibility, curiosity‐exploration and flourishing over time (Study 3). Findings align majority‐group acculturation with key priorities of HE and government programmes.

items.title: Intergroup Competition Promotes Intragroup Cooperation: A Meta-Analysis of Social Dilemmas
items.abstract: Current theories pose that intergroup competition elevates intragroup cooperation and put forward hypotheses about conditions that increase the magnitude of this effect. Here, we report a preregistered meta-analysis of studies using experimental games that manipulate the presence of intergroup competition and its effect on intragroup cooperation. Our investigation reveals the overall direction and magnitude of the effect, which addresses mixed empirical findings. We identified 25 articles to meet inclusion criteria, which yielded 70 effect sizes. A multilevel random effects model revealed a medium positive effect of intergroup competition on intragroup cooperation ( g = .677, N = 6,051). Studies involving intergroup competition with interdependence produced a strong effect, whereas this effect was weaker for studies without interdependence. Our findings present meta-analytic evidence that intergroup competition promotes intragroup cooperation and identify opportunities for future research.

items.title: Exploring Cultural and Individual Differences in the Hierarchy of Moral Concern: Evidence From Student Samples Across 41 Cultural Groups
items.abstract: Many important historical and contemporary ethical debates (e.g., on slavery, abortion and environmental protection) reflect disagreements about what we owe to different groups of individuals. Recent work in moral psychology has uncovered a seemingly replicable hierarchy of moral concern, but these studies were conducted in a few countries from the Anglosphere, raising doubts about cross‐cultural generalizability. Here, we analysed a data set with 6561 university students from 41 cultural groups to explore cultural and individual variation in moral concern. We find that (1) on average, across the 41 cultural groups, 11 of the 13 rankings in the typical hierarchy of moral concern replicated, pointing to substantial cultural similarities; (2) groups that are culturally more similar to the United States showed a pattern that was more similar to the pattern observed in the initial US studies; and (3) cultural differences were most pronounced when examining people's relative concern for non‐human animals and the environment.

items.title: Underestimating Honesty in Distributive Negotiations: Misjudging Counterparts’ Motivations
items.abstract: Negotiators often face two dilemmas: whether to be honest and whether to believe their counterpart is honest. We propose a discrepancy in how negotiators approach these dilemmas, leading to an expected versus actual honesty gap. When deciding whether to be honest, negotiators are influenced not only by self-interest but also by moral identity concerns, which promote honesty. However, when deciding whether counterparts are honest, negotiators assume they are primarily motivated by self-interest and thus overestimate their dishonesty. Five studies examining online secondhand market negotiations found buyers often underestimated sellers' honesty, and this was accounted for by their misperceptions of sellers' motivations. While sellers tended to be honest because of moral identity concerns, buyers expected them to be driven primarily by self-interest. The actual-expected honesty gap was particularly prevalent when sellers' moral identity concerns were situationally activated, and altering buyers' perceptions of sellers' motivations reduced the gap. Findings further suggest potential targeted interventions to foster trust.

items.title: National Football Teams’ Performance Predicts Spectators’ Identities, Affect and Sociopolitical Attitudes: An Investigation During the 2024 EURO Tournament
items.abstract: On the basis of two social‐affective frameworks, we posited that national football team performance (winning vs. losing) would impact spectators’ identities, affect and sociopolitical attitudes—including their intergroup attitudes (i.e., in‐group favouritism and multiculturalism) and societal perceptions (i.e., national optimism, perceived crisis severity, political trust and perceived racism). During the UEFA EURO 2024 tournament in Germany, we assessed residents ( N = 1012) from five participating countries before the tournament (baseline) and after each game. Confirming our preregistered hypotheses, national team wins led to stronger national identification, which, in turn, predicted more in‐group favouritism and less support for multiculturalism. Wins also predicted more positive affect, which then coincided with stronger national optimism. Contrary to our hypotheses, however, no direct effects emerged for spectators’ political trust, nor their perceptions of crisis severity and racism. These findings highlight ways in which national sports experiences can predict spectators’ collective identities, emotions and selected sociopolitical attitudes.

items.title: Everyone Knows It's a Hoax: The Role of Perceived Descriptive Norms in Conspiracy Beliefs
items.abstract: People's belief in conspiracy theories is shaped by social influence processes. This contribution investigated these processes in six studies (total N = 2906) by examining the role of descriptive norms, that is, the perception that others endorse conspiracy theories. Studies 1a and 1b indicate that stronger own conspiracy beliefs are associated with overestimating conspiracy beliefs in others. Studies 2a and 2b showed that experimentally exposing participants to a conspiracy theory increased their perceptions of the extent others believed this conspiracy theory. Studies 3 and 4 manipulated descriptive norm information. Although abstract, context‐free normative information did not influence conspiracy beliefs (Study 3), providing factual statistical information showing that most people do not believe in various specific conspiracy theories reduced participants’ own conspiracy beliefs (Study 4). These results indicate that perceived descriptive norms are important to understand why people often believe the conspiracy theories spread by others.

items.title: Helpful and in Danger: Attributes and Correlates of Perceived Occupational Heroism
items.abstract: Some occupations such as firefighters are described as heroic, while others, such as healthcare workers, are applauded as “heroes” in crises. In two preregistered correlational studies conducted on representative U.K. samples, we evaluated theory-based attributes of occupational heroism, and its relationship to specific policy-relevant attitudes toward occupations. In Study 1 ( N = 430), we confirmed that occupational heroism relates to the perceived helpfulness and risk exposure of workers. In Study 2 ( N = 840), we further showed that occupational heroism is associated with a moral shield: workers’ hero status correlates with decreased acceptability of criticism toward them, and increased support for deregulating them and protecting them from punishment for rule-breaking. Unlike previous findings suggesting a willingness to exploit heroized workers, heroism correlated with increased gratitude toward workers, support for their demands, and perception that they are vulnerable. Societal consequences and relevance for policy-making are discussed.

items.title: Perceived time in the presence of others: Further arguments for an attentional view of social facilitation
items.abstract: Although the effects of the presence of others on behavior constitute one of the oldest topics studied in social psychology, the reason why these effects occur is still the subject of scientific debate. Three hypotheses are commonly cited: (1) the presence of others facilitates dominant responses by increasing arousal, (2) it captures attention, or (3) it increases the efforts of those being observed. Few studies have attempted to distinguish between these explanations, and those that have done so have used a specific paradigm: the Stroop task. In the present study, we proposed an alternative approach based on the use of the temporal bisection task. In three studies, the bisection results showed a temporal shortening effect in social presence (that of an experimenter) consistent with an attentional distraction-related effect. Our results also provided the first evidence that this effect may be stronger when the attentional conflict between the task and the presence is unimodal (e.g., visual task and visual presence) rather than cross-modal (e.g., auditive task and visual presence). They also suggested that the social presence effect might be similar to that produced by a mechanical distractor, although the social nature of the distractor increased the attention-related effect. We discuss how variations in the presence and behavior of the experimenter could contribute to the difficulty of replicating certain studies in experimental psychology, given that the social presence of the experimenter is generally assumed to be innocuous.

items.title: Sustaining your stance by speaking your mind: Expressing moral judgments increases certainty and prevents moral desensitization
items.abstract: When news about another person's wrongdoing goes viral, people will hear about it repeatedly through social and traditional media outlets. Prior research suggests that this repeated exposure reduces how unethical people think the wrongdoing is – a moral repetition effect . The present research reveals that repetition no longer reduces moral condemnation when people express moral judgments upon each exposure, as they often do in the real world by commenting on news about wrongdoing. Drawing on attitudes research, we argue that repeatedly expressing moral judgments eliminates the moral repetition effect by increasing how certain people feel about their judgments. We found support in a meta-analysis ( k = 13 experiments, N = 6548 participants) and three pre-registered experiments ( N = 2637). The meta-analysis finds a smaller moral repetition effect for wrongdoings that tend to make people feel more (vs. less) certain about their moral judgments. Experiment 1 finds that people hold their moral judgments about a repeatedly encountered wrongdoing with more certainty when they actively express these judgments on each encounter. Experiments 2 and 3 show that prompting people to repeatedly express their moral judgments eliminates the moral repetition effect. These findings deepen our understanding of how and when repetition erodes moral condemnation and offer an actionable strategy to counteract repetition's effects. Encouraging people to express their views – rather than just to passively consume information – may help prevent moral desensitization to wrongdoing.

items.title: Between law and conscience: Act legality shapes moral evaluation
items.abstract: Can legality shape moral judgment? Across four experiments (N = 1,559), participants judged identical actions as more morally wrong when they were described as illegal rather than “not illegal.” This effect extended to judgments of moral character: individuals who performed illegal actions were evaluated more negatively than those who performed otherwise identical legal actions. The influence of legality was robust across several contexts, emerging even when agents violated the law unintentionally, when laws were imposed by a totalitarian government, and when actions were described as socially accepted by the majority of local residents. At the same time, legality exerted a stronger influence when it aligned with prevailing social norms and among participants who more strongly endorsed respect for authority as a moral good. We propose that people commonly use legality as a heuristic cue when evaluating the morality of actions and actors. Together, these findings suggest that legal frameworks not only reflect public opinion but also shape how people judge the morality of actions and those who perform them.

items.title: How and why the omission bias affects victims' and third parties' responses to interpersonal transgressions
items.abstract: Prior research has identified an omission bias whereby third-party observers attribute greater intent, responsibility, and immorality to a transgressor for their harmful commissions than their harmful omissions. However, this research has not examined whether victims also show an omission bias in response to an interpersonal transgression committed against them, and whether these perceptions affect the apology-forgiveness process. We conducted four experiments (Ns = 376; 593; 595; 813) using complementary methods (hypothetical standardized offenses and real-life transgressions) to examine how and why commission and omission transgressions differentially affect victims’ forgiveness, and whether apologies are differentially effective at eliciting forgiveness for these transgressions. We found that forgiveness was generally lower for commission (vs. omission) transgressions. Moreover, victims perceived commission (vs. omission) transgressions as higher in responsibility and intent, and these offense perceptions in turn predicted reduced forgiveness, both on their own and serially through judgments of immorality. However, apologizing (vs. not apologizing) predicted greater forgiveness for both types of offenses. In Study 4, we also tested whether victims’ perceptions of commissions and omissions differed from third-party observers’ perceptions. The effect of the commission (vs. omission) transgression on offense perceptions, moral judgments, and apology-forgiveness was similar across victim and third-party observer perspectives. These studies demonstrate how and why forgiveness might be less forthcoming for commissions than omissions, but provide evidence that apologies confer benefits for both types of offenses.

items.title: Disability Representation in Social and Personality Psychology Research: A State-of-the-Art Review
items.abstract: We conducted a systematic state-of-the-field review examining disability representation of three flagship social and personality psychology journals between 2017 and 2022. First, we examined how frequently publications used disability-related terminology, finding that 192 of the 2,343 articles surveyed did so. Second, we examined patterns of disability-related terminology use and found that these concepts were most often used in an extraneous manner (e.g., in parenthetical phrases). Only 3 articles were primarily focused on disability. This is the first systematic investigation to examine how and to what extent social and personality psychology research addresses topics related to disability. These findings highlight a need for substantive change in the representation of disability within social and personality psychology. We close with recommendations for researchers.

items.title: Seeing to Connect: How Visual and Auditory Channels Shape Empathic Interactions
items.abstract: This research examines how visual and auditory channels affect empathic interactions from the perspectives of the listener (the empathy provider), the storyteller (the empathy recipient), and the shared dyadic experience. Across three pre-registered studies ( N = 710), storytellers shared emotional experiences with listeners through online video calls, with cameras on or off. Study 1 examined empathic accuracy, attentiveness, empathy, and togetherness. Study 2 replicated these findings and extended them to emotional congruency. Study 3 introduced vocal responsiveness, positivity resonance, and prosocial behavior. Auditory information alone was sufficient for listeners to accurately identify storytellers’ emotions and to maintain high self-reported attentiveness and empathy. However, visual information shaped how storytellers perceived their listeners, and was key to creating shared positive emotions, we-ness, and mutual care, and appeared to enhance prosocial behavior. These findings suggest that while hearing each other might suffice for information sharing, optimal empathic connection requires seeing and being seen.

items.title: To Regulate or Not to Regulate? Situational and Individual Differences in Emotion Regulation Initiation in Daily Life
items.abstract: Situational and individual differences shape how and why people regulate emotions but whether emotion regulation is initiated remains understudied. We hypothesize that, for example, less familiar situations might be associated with more regulation initiation and people who believe emotions are controllable initiate regulation more frequently. Using experience sampling (N = 216; 7x/14 days), we found participants initiated regulation 60% of the time over the past two hours. As predicted, people initiated regulation in less familiar, less pleasant contexts, and with more dominant, less warm social partners. Unexpectedly, individuals who believe emotions are uncontrollable were more likely to initiate regulation, even after accounting for affect. These findings highlight that while attention has mostly focused on strategy selection or efficacy, meaningful situational and individual differences also exist at the emotion regulation initiation stage when individuals determine whether to expend regulatory resources to maintain well-being.

items.title: Objectified and Opting Out: How Experiencing Objectification Steers Students Away From Challenging Careers
items.abstract: While the psychological consequences of experiencing objectification are well-documented, its impact on early career decision-making remains largely unexplored. To address this gap, we investigated whether being objectified steers college students away from challenging jobs. Across six studies ( N = 1,584), we found consistent evidence that experiencing objectification leads students to “opt out” and avoid challenging jobs. Correlational data showed that students’ experiences of being objectified were associated with their challenge avoidance in intended (Pilot Study) and actual (Study 1) career decisions. In Study 2, we experimentally manipulated objectification and found that participants in the objectification condition showed greater avoidance of challenging jobs. Study 3 showed that this relationship was mediated by reduced perceived control. Studies 4a and 4b further validated this mediating role by using a causal chain design. Our findings shed light on the social cognitive factors that influence career decision-making.

items.title: The Impact of Regulatory Goals on the Disclosure of Self-presentational Vulnerabilities
items.abstract: Individuals often disclose their self-presentational vulnerabilities, including the use of counterfeit products or weight-loss medications. Yet, despite the commonality of such vulnerable self-disclosure, little is known about who discloses, why they do so, and when they choose to reveal or conceal these vulnerabilities. Addressing that gap, we examine how regulatory focus and relationship closeness jointly shape the disclosure of self-presentational vulnerabilities.
