Across eight studies, we find that prevention-focused (vs. promotion-focused) individuals are more willing to disclose self-presentational vulnerabilities to close others, but not to distant others. We further find that this effect occurs because prevention-focused (vs. promotion-focused) individuals more strongly believe that disclosing such vulnerable information to close others can strengthen their interpersonal relationships.

items.title: Being Observed by a Tutor Enhances Foreign Speech Production Learning in Video-Mediated Training
items.abstract: Social presence, particularly awareness of being observed by a tutor, may enhance learners’ engagement and attention during foreign language practice, but its effects on learning and associated neural activity remain poorly understood. We investigated whether learners’ (n = 32) awareness of being observed by a tutor influences foreign speech learning in a short (11-min) video-mediated listen-and-repeat training for Mandarin words. In the online group, learners knew the tutor could see them, whereas in the offline group, they knew the tutor could neither see nor hear them. Tone production was assessed before, during, and after training, and tone identification before and after training. Electroencephalography and autonomic activity were recorded during training. Tone production accuracy improved from pre- to post-training in the online group only, whereas tone identification improved similarly in both groups. Posterior alpha power increased during training in the offline group but did not change significantly in the online group. Together, these findings suggest that awareness of being observed by a tutor may support foreign language speech production learning in video-mediated settings. The accompanying differences in posterior alpha activity further indicate that the social context of learning is associated with differences in neural activity during practice.

items.title: Workplace Relationships and Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Generative AI is now embedded in how coworkers, leaders, and organizations communicate, yet its effects on the relationships among them are still poorly understood. This review synthesizes recent research on how an individual’s AI use changes the way others perceive, judge, and behave toward them, and shows that these effects can be explained by established theories of human-human interaction, including attribution theory, computers-as-social-actors, the integrative model of organizational trust, social exchange theory, and resource-based theories. The evidence suggests that observers often read AI use as a sign of disposition rather than circumstance, judging AI users as less competent, motivated, warm, and authentic, and that disclosure does not repair the resulting loss of trust. These perceptions carry over into behavior: coworkers reciprocate less, share less knowledge, and show less prosocial behavior toward AI users, while AI-related job insecurity, loneliness, and work alienation further strain ties among colleagues. AI use also loosens moral standards and shifts how blame is assigned, making people more critical of others’ work but more lenient toward misconduct. These effects are conditional rather than uniformly negative. AI can reduce loneliness, improve coordination, and prompt employees to invest more in emotionally supportive ties, and relational buffers such as leader-member exchange, shared leadership, and supervisor support can offset its costs. The review concludes that AI’s costs to workplace relationships run mainly through indirect pathways, not through the technology itself. It outlines organizational implications, including clear norms for when and why AI is used and protection of socially valued tasks, and identifies priorities for future research: longitudinal designs, team- and network-level studies, intervention research, and more diverse samples.

items.title: Coupled social dilemmas reveal positive cross-game transfer in humans and contrasting cue use in tested GPT agents
items.abstract: Cooperation across social settings requires deciding whether to reciprocate a partner’s helpful behavior or exploit it when incentives change. We examined this tension in an online experiment with 430 participants playing a Prisoner’s Dilemma (PD), either alone or followed by a Snowdrift game (SD), where defection pays more against a sufficiently likely cooperator. We also placed programmed bots—computer-controlled players following a fixed rule—in some groups. By programming them to cooperate in PD and reciprocate their partner’s PD action in SD, we created a consistent source of cooperation and reciprocity. This allowed us to ask whether humans also cooperated more with one another. Humans cooperated more in SD after their partner cooperated in PD, even when observed partner behavior made defection the better immediate material response. This pattern is consistent with reciprocity, although choices do not identify beliefs or motives. Human–human cooperation was higher in groups containing bots; coupling alone produced no detected increase in mean PD cooperation. Separate experiments with GPT language-model agents asked whether frequent cooperation was accompanied by similar responses across games. Despite high PD cooperation, partner PD cooperation predicted less GPT cooperation in SD in the primary pooled analysis. This association varied across configurations and did not generally indicate payoff-maximizing choices. Simulations using fitted human response rules illustrated the possible effects of alternative bot policies. These findings reveal responses to cooperative partners across contexts that overall cooperation rates can obscure.

items.title: Only Your Mind Sets the Limits: Socio‐Cognitive Pathways between Growth Mindset and Reading Achievement Across Nordic and Chinese Educational Systems
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Mindset theory has increasingly shifted from asking whether growth mindsets predict achievement to asking how, for whom, and under what conditions beliefs about intelligence become motivationally consequential. AIMS: This study contributes to that theoretical shift by examining mindset as a distal belief embedded within a broader social-cognitive system of achievement motivation. SAMPLE AND METHODS: Using PISA 2018 data on 36,905 15-year-old students in Denmark, Finland, Sweden, Hong Kong, and Beijing-Shanghai-Jiangsu-Zhejiang, China, we modeled associations among mindset, socioeconomic background, mastery goals, motivation to master school tasks, reading self-concept, general self-efficacy, fear of failure, and reading achievement through a multi-group path analysis approach. RESULTS: Model results showed that a growth mindset was positively associated with reading achievement in the Nordic countries, unrelated to achievement in Hong Kong, and negatively associated with achievement in B-S-J-Z China. Indirect effects were generally small, while reading self-concept emerged as the most consistent proximal correlate of achievement. These patterns suggest that mindset is best understood not as a universal predictor of achievement but as a context-sensitive component within culturally situated socio-cognitive systems. CONCLUSIONS: The study, therefore, uses cross-national evidence to refine the theoretical placement of mindset within achievement motivation, highlighting the importance of mechanisms, proximal competence beliefs, and cultural boundary conditions.

items.title: Happy or redundant? Retrieval practice enhances lasting learning in non-interactive teaching for low-quality explanations
items.abstract: Background Supporting lasting learning is a central goal in education, particularly in schools where long-term retention is crucial for students' academic success. Generative learning helps construct meaningful mental representations, while retrieval practice supports consolidation and long-term retention. Combining both strategies may foster learning; however, research remains scarce. Aims We investigated how combining generative activities and retrieval practice affects students' conceptual knowledge and monitoring accuracy in authentic school settings for immediate and lasting learning. Additionally, we explored associations between generation, retrieval, and explanation quality (i.e., completeness, elaboration, correctness). Sample The classroom experiment was conducted in authentic physics lessons with N = 344 secondary students. Methods Students participated in a physics teaching unit about converging lenses and were randomly assigned within each class to one of four combinations of sequential learning activities crossing two factors (non-generation vs. generation; non-retrieval vs. retrieval). Conceptual knowledge and monitoring accuracy were measured immediately and after eight weeks. Results Conceptual knowledge and monitoring accuracy did not significantly differ between generation, retrieval, or their sequential combination at either test. However, exploratory analyses revealed that retrieval practice supported lasting learning when prior generative processing was of low quality—that is, when students' explanations were incomplete, less elaborated, or inaccurate. Conclusions Combining generation and retrieval does not universally enhance learning. Its effectiveness appears to depend on the quality of prior generative processing. In this sense, retrieval practice may serve a happy role—compensating for fragile knowledge—or a redundant one, offering no added benefit when prior understanding is already strong.

items.title: When Fine is Large and Gross is Small: A Meta-Analysis of Links Between Fine and Gross Motor Skills with Academic-Cognitive Skills
items.abstract: Researchers and practitioners often emphasize the importance of fine motor skills (FiMS) and gross motor skills (GMS) for academic and cognitive development. However, no systematic review of empirical evidence has compared the associations between FiMS and GMS for key academic-cognitive domains (i.e., reading, writing, mathematics, language, general academic, and cognitive skills). A literature search in five databases identified 59 eligible correlational studies measuring both FiMS and GMS ( k = 856, N = 40,806) from an initial selection of 34,811 articles. Mixed effects meta-regressions, controlling for methodological and sample factors, revealed moderate to strong correlations between FiMS and writing, reading, mathematics, and general academic skills, as well as moderate links with cognition and language. GMS displayed small to moderate associations with reading, writing, mathematics, language, and cognitive skills, but no statistically significant links to general academic skills. Overall, FiMS showed more substantial correlations with academic-cognitive skills ( r = .302) than GMS did ( r = .170, p < .001), although the associations were more similar for language and executive functions compared to those for intelligence. Practical implications are discussed with respect to the role motor skills play in child and adolescent education.

items.title: Replicating the advantage of classifying over generating examples in an authentic relational category learning context
items.abstract: Educators use psychological knowledge about categories to adapt their teaching to learners. Learning these categories usually requires understanding the underlying relational structures. To learn relational categories, learning tasks should effectively foster generalization and discrimination processes. Previous research indicates that tasks requiring learners to generate their own examples are less effective for learning relational categories and more likely to elicit overestimation of learning than tasks requiring learners to classify provided examples. We conducted an experiment with N = 104 students in degree programs that encompass educational science to investigate whether the disadvantage of generating examples in contrast to classifying examples can be mitigated by deliberately promoting generalization and discrimination processes during learning. The experiment was designed to reflect an authentic context for learning relational categories and to assess how students apply these categories in real-world settings. The results showed that despite the deliberate promotion of generalization and discrimination processes, classifying provided examples was still more effective for learning relational categories. Classifying examples presumably fosters a high level of cognitive engagement while simultaneously providing instructional guidance. In contrast, generating examples may offer insufficient guidance and thereby restrict learning. Moreover, students who generated examples during learning not only overestimated their learning but the overestimation also persisted throughout the knowledge test and after its completion. Based on the findings, educators should consider using classification tasks rather than generation tasks when teaching relational categories while also taking into account both learning and metacognitive processes.

items.title: Key arithmetic word problems to assess children's understanding
items.abstract: Structured abstract Background Solving arithmetic word problems is an essential mathematical skill that many children find challenging. The difficulty often depends on how well the problem framing aligns with children's prior knowledge, which can either support or hinder its interpretation. The ability to extract meaningful information even from counterintuitive problems indicates a profound understanding and mastery of problem-solving. Aims This study investigated how problem framing influences children's individual performance on arithmetic word problems, aiming to identify tasks most effective for diagnosing students needing additional support. A further aim was to explore how improvements in solving non-intuitive addition problems carry over to later-introduced subtraction problems. Sample The sample consisted of 544 children using an application designed to help first graders solve arithmetic word problems. Methods Latent Profile Analysis was applied to identify distinct response patterns across problems that differed in contextual congruency. Subsequent analyses examined performance on subtraction problems after addition practice. Results The analysis revealed three distinct profiles that varied most significantly for specific problems, for which the framing did not match the solver's intuition, namely problems incongruent with the substitution and scenario analogy. Such problems could thus be used to identify children who have difficulties fully integrating mathematical concepts. Evidence that improvement in performance on non-intuitive addition problems was related to later-introduced subtraction performance was also observed for specific problem types. Conclusion These findings support the SECO model, showing that children's performance depends on how well problems align with different analogies, offering a new way to understand variation of problem difficulties within traditional problem frameworks. Counterintuitive problems are good candidates to efficiently identify children who have difficulty fully integrating mathematical concepts.

items.title: Associations between maths ability mindset, maths task preference and physiological responses to feedback during an arithmetic task across two primary school years
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Students' mindsets, reactions to feedback and learning-related behaviour are important for academic success, yet little is known about how these factors and their interconnections develop during primary school. AIMS: To explore longitudinal associations between students' mindsets, physiological responses to performance feedback, and task preference in maths across two primary school years. SAMPLE: Eighty-nine students were followed from grade 3 to grade 4. METHODS: During the autumn term of both grades, students' mindsets were assessed using a questionnaire. After a challenging maths task, students chose their next task-either another challenging one to learn more or an easy task to succeed. Skin conductance was recorded during an arithmetic task with performance feedback. Mixed-effects models were used to analyse associations and their development. RESULTS: We found that growth-minded students preferred the challenging task in both grades, yet mindset did not relate to feedback-related physiological responses. Task preference demonstrated only partly marginal associations with these responses and only in the beginning of the task. Specifically, students preferring the challenging task showed a smaller and faster-habituating physiological reaction to feedback at task onset. CONCLUSIONS: Physiological responses and mindset had unique relations with task preference, suggesting the potential importance of both in learning. Associations with only initial physiological responses and their habituation, not overall feedback-related responses, suggest subtle temporal changes in physiological reactions during educational activities. The present findings, although requiring replication, suggest that supporting students in regulating performance-related arousal at task onset may be particularly important.

items.title: Germane processes moderate the effectiveness of complex desirable difficulty tasks
items.abstract: Although there is abundant empirical evidence that, separately applied, cognitive load theory and desirable difficulty theory enhance performance, little is known about how these theories can be successfully combined. To address this critical gap, the present study investigated the effects of complexity (constantly high vs. gradually increasing) and desirable difficulty (interleaved vs. blocked) on performance, metacognitive strategy use, and self- and task perception. In total, 132 learners participated in this 2 × 2 factorial intervention study. This study consisted of a main learning session and a posttest two days later. The posttest results showed that confronting learners with complex desirable difficulty tasks was effective in fostering performance. Furthermore, cognitive load was revealed as one of the major reasons for learners’ metacognitive engagement. We discuss the implications of these findings for research, theory, and practice and provide recommendations for future research.

items.title: Effects and Characteristics of Mathematics Interventions for Students with Co-Occurring Difficulties in Mathematics and Reading: A Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis
items.abstract: Among students who have learning difficulties in mathematics and reading, co-occurring difficulties in both domains are highly prevalent. Research has shown that students with co-occurring mathematics and reading difficulties tend to have greater cognitive challenges than students who have difficulties with either mathematics or reading. It is plausible that these cognitive difficulties can influence the responsiveness to interventions. This systematic review with meta-analysis investigated the effects and characteristics of mathematics interventions in early elementary students (G1-G3) with co-occurring difficulties in mathematics and reading, as well as how these students had been identified in the included studies. Based on a comprehensive literature search, only nine studies ( k = 1036) met the predefined inclusion criteria. The available evidence indicates a positive overall mean effect of mathematics interventions on mathematical outcomes for students with co-occurring mathematics and reading difficulties ( g = 0.47 for the model with outliers; g = 0.52 for the model without outliers). However, this result should be interpreted with caution, given the heterogeneity of the evidence and the relatively small evidence base. The synthesis of intervention characteristics highlighted that effective mathematics interventions commonly included explicit instruction, which was classified as potentially relevant for low-performing students, as well as overall structure, repetition, and strategy learning, which were classified as potentially relevant to support executive function. Finally, findings revealed considerable variation in the cut-off criteria used to identify students with co-occurring mathematics and reading difficulties. Implications of the findings and directions for future research are discussed.

items.title: Infusing students’ everyday experiences in classrooms: a case study of classroom conversations in life skills education
items.abstract: In recent years, the importance of developing instructional designs in schools to enhance students’ life skills has received increased attention. Placing life skills related issues on the curriculum implies that students’ personal lives and experiences are being given a more prominent role in education. However, while existing empirical studies have revealed valuable insights into aspects relevant to the practice of teaching life skills, there is lack of research on how teachers guide students in situ within life skills education settings. In this study, we explore how teachers orient to students’ personal experiences, ideas and assumptions from their everyday lives during classroom conversations in the context of life skills education. Specifically, we examine the opportunities and challenges teachers might face in this type of instructional work. Our analysis draws on video data from a life skills project in which lower secondary school students and their teachers engaged in classroom conversations about issues related to youth, identity and belonging. The analysis shows (1) how the teachers sometimes used students’ personal experiences as resources for guiding their conceptual understanding, (2) the efforts required of teachers to handle emotional and sometimes sensitive student contributions in whole-class conversations and (3) the challenges teachers sometimes faced in integrating conceptual knowledge with students’ everyday experiences. We discuss these findings in relation to the existing literature.

items.title: A systematic review on the development of self-regulated learning
items.abstract: This systematic review investigates the developmental trajectory of self-regulated learning (SRL), emphasizing its critical role in academic and lifelong learning. Despite its importance, limited understanding exists regarding SRL's progression across different educational stages and the factors influencing its development. The review synthesizes current research, revealing a clear developmental pattern where executive functions (EF) and metacognitive knowledge become more sophisticated from early childhood through primary school. However, a concerning decline in SRL strategy use is observed during the transition from primary to secondary school, despite continued improvement in metacognitive knowledge and accuracy. This decline, identified through both cross-sectional and longitudinal studies, challenges the assumption that SRL naturally improves with age, highlighting the need for targeted interventions during this critical transition period. The findings underscore the importance of early and sustained support for SRL development, informing educational practices and policies aimed at fostering these skills. The review also emphasizes the necessity for future research to employ rigorous methodologies, longitudinal designs, and consider contextual and motivational factors to deepen our understanding of SRL development. By elucidating these developmental processes, the review contributes to the advancement of educational theory and practice, with significant implications for promoting academic success and lifelong learning. The insights gained from this review highlight the multifaceted and dynamic nature of SRL development, advocating for targeted educational interventions to support the cultivation of self-regulation skills in children and adolescents.

items.title: Concrete images, diverse ideas: The role of pictures in learning from multimedia texts of varying abstractness
items.abstract: Background Knowledge abstractness is one of the factors affecting learning outcomes, particularly in learning from multimedia texts. However, most previous studies on multimedia learning have focused on manipulating pictorial abstractness, while the role of text topic abstractness remains largely unexplored. Aims 1. Examine how topic abstractness influences multimedia learning outcomes when pictorial abstractness remains constant. 2. Investigate how this effect manifests across testing tasks targeting different outcomes of multimedia learning. Sample Sixty four university students (18-32 years, M = 21.4; 81% female, 19% male; all native Russian speakers). Methods We conducted a within-subject experiment, which included learning and testing stages. During the learning stage, participants read one abstract and one concrete multimedia text. The testing stage consisted of a series of tasks, including Recognition , Verification , Transfer , Concept Definition , and Summary . Results Participants performed better on the Picture Recognition , Verification , Transfer , and Concept Definition tasks after learning from the concrete text compared to the abstract one. However, no significant differences were observed between the two texts in performance on the Text Recognition and Summary tasks. Conclusions In line with the concreteness effect, participants generally performed more efficiently on post-reading tests after learning from the concrete text compared to the abstract one. This effect may be attributed to insufficient processing of pictures embedded in the abstract text. However, the equal performance on Summary for both abstract and concrete texts further clarifies the findings and suggests that the effect of topic abstractness on multimedia learning outcomes is non-linear.

items.title: Fixed mindset‐signalling peer behaviours predict impostor feelings and evaluative concerns
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Beliefs that ability is fixed can make challenges feel like evidence of inadequacy rather than opportunities to learn. Peers play a powerful role in communicating these beliefs through their everyday words and behaviours, yet prior research has relied primarily on cross-sectional surveys or hypothetical scenarios. AIMS: This research examined how peers' mindset-signalling behaviours relate to impostor feelings and evaluative concerns as they unfold in daily life and as they are remembered. SAMPLES: Study 1 included 130 undergraduates (670 daily reports) enrolled in at least one STEM course, and Study 2 drew on follow-up interviews with 18 of these students. METHODS: Study 1 used a 10-day daily diary design with Bayesian multilevel modelling to examine within-day associations between peer behaviours, impostor feelings and evaluative concerns. Study 2 used retrospective interviews to explore how students interpreted and made meaning of these experiences. RESULTS: On days when students observed peers expressing fixed-mindset cues, such as fixed-ability statements or self-deprecating remarks, they reported higher levels of impostor feelings and evaluative concerns. Observing peers persist through difficulty predicted lower impostor feelings that day. Retrospective interviews echoed these patterns, although different moments stood out in memory. Students most often recalled peers sharing their struggles or offering help as emotionally meaningful experiences. CONCLUSIONS: Peer mindset signals matter both in daily experience and in later memory. Daily verbal cues were associated with same-day impostor feelings and evaluative concerns, whereas remembered moments of vulnerability and support became incorporated into broader emotional narratives.

items.title: Longitudinal and differential effects of differentiated instruction on academic achievement and subjective well-being in inclusive secondary education
items.abstract: Background Differentiated instruction (DI) is a fundamental component of teaching quality, particularly in diverse and inclusive classrooms. While DI has been shown to enhance students' academic achievement, research at the secondary education level remains limited, and its impact on students’ subjective well-being—widely recognized as essential for learning—has been largely unexplored. Moreover, effects may differ for students with special educational needs in learning (SEN-L). Aim This study investigated cross-sectional and longitudinal effects of classroom-level DI practices on students’ academic achievement and subjective well-being in lower secondary education, incorporating both student and teacher perspectives. Additionally, it examined whether the effects of DI differ between students with and without SEN-L. Sample Data were drawn from a longitudinal study with three measurement occasions (Grades 6, 7, and 9). The sample comprised 4654 sixth-grade students, along with 417 German and 398 mathematics teachers. Methods Multilevel regression analyses with latent variables were conducted to investigate cross-sectional effects. To examine longitudinal effects, latent neighbor change models were applied. Results Cross-sectionally, DI showed some small positive associations with academic achievement and, particularly student-reported DI, small positive associations with subjective well-being. DI predicted some changes in both outcomes over time, albeit inconsistently and with small-to-negligible effect sizes. The findings indicate only two small differential effects for students with SEN-L compared to other students. Conclusions The study extends research on DI by focusing on both students’ academic achievement and subjective well-being in lower secondary education, while calling for continued research into its longitudinal effects and underlying mechanisms.

items.title: Reciprocal relations between teachers' relational goals, students' conflict and boredom in German and mathematics classes
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Teachers' relational goals are important prerequisites of positive teacher-student relationships, in turn shaping students' emotional experiences during the learning process. However, the reciprocal nature of these interrelations remains unclear. AIMS: We tested reciprocal relations between teachers' relational goals, student-perceived conflicts with teachers, and students' boredom in German and mathematics class. SAMPLE: N = 89 German language teachers with their n = 1573 students and n = 77 mathematics teachers with their n = 1588 students who participated across four time points (T1-T4) over two school years. METHODS: We estimated two subject-specific (German/mathematics) random-intercept cross-lagged panel models (RI-CLPMs). RESULTS: In German classes, teachers' relational goals (T3) negatively related to students' boredom (T4). In mathematics classes, students' boredom (T1) negatively related to teachers' relational goals (T2). In both subjects, students' overall conflict with the teacher was positively related to their overall boredom. CONCLUSIONS: The findings suggest subject-specific transactional dynamics rather than consistent reciprocal effects by showing that German language teachers' relational goals are related to lower subsequent boredom, whereas in mathematics, higher student boredom was associated with lower subsequent teachers' relational goals. Strengthening relational classroom practices may help reduce boredom and conflict.

items.title: Professional vision and medical education: dividing diagnoses into categories to support more effective learning in dermatology
items.abstract: Background Proficiency in interpretation of visual findings, professional vision, plays an essential role in the doctor's profession. Thus, learning visual features from images is a key curricular component of medical education, for example, in radiology and dermatology. Nevertheless, there is scarcity of research on professional vision in dermatology. Aims The aims of this study were to 1) measure how professional vision differs before and after a dermatology course, and if there are differences across diagnoses, 2) cluster different diagnoses based on learning patterns, 3) investigate the development of students’ accuracy, decision times and confidence within different categories. Sample Participants were 394 medical students and 7 experts. Methods Participants completed an online perceptual learning module at three timepoints (pre, mid and post) during a course. The task was to recognize a visually presented dermatological condition and choose the correct diagnosis from eight options and rate the confidence in decision. The module contained 47 different diagnoses, each presented once. Students repeated the modules multiple times. A two-parameter Item-Response-Theory model was fitted to the data. Based on item characteristic curves, the diagnoses were clustered into eight categories. Results Diagnostic accuracy, decision times and confidence improved in most, but not all, pre-mid and mid-post comparisons. There were major differences in learning patterns (amount and pace of improvement) across the eight categories. Conclusions The differences between diagnosis categories were larger than differences between individual participants. This finding can be utilized in medical education by focusing teaching resources on diagnoses that are difficult to learn.

items.title: Social relationships and emotional experiences during classroom learning: Exploring students' physiological activation patterns
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Most research on students' emotional experiences during classroom learning relies on self-reports, which provide limited access to physiological processes associated with emotional experiences. Accordingly, researchers have called for complementary methodological approaches, such as physiological measures. AIMS: Therefore, this study assessed students' algorithm-derived physiological activation patterns as proxy measures associated with emotional experiences during classroom learning and examined the extent to which these patterns are related to the quality of student-teacher relationships and peer relationships. SAMPLE: The sample consists of 154 secondary school students. Students were physiologically monitored across four different subjects. METHODS: Self-report instruments were used to assess students' social relationship quality. During lessons, students wore sensor wristbands continuously recording electrodermal activity, skin temperature and movement-related signals. Based on these multimodal signals, the bands' algorithm derived two high-arousal physiological activation patterns (i.e., appetitive and aversive) and two low-arousal physiological activation patterns (i.e., attention and passivity). These patterns were aggregated at lesson-level and analysed in relation to social relationship quality using multilevel models. RESULTS: More positive peer and student-teacher relationships were associated with fewer aversive activation patterns, whereas appetitive activation patterns showed no associations. Passivity patterns were negatively associated with peer relationships, whereas attention patterns showed no associations. CONCLUSIONS: The study provides initial evidence that students' social relationship quality is associated with algorithm-derived physiological activation patterns during authentic classroom learning. More broadly, the study highlights the potential benefits of complementing self-report measures with ambulatory physiological assessments to better understand how social and emotional processes are intertwined in classroom learning.

items.title: From Body to Word: A Three-Level Meta-Analysis of Embodied Vocabulary Learning
items.abstract: Embodied cognition posits that cognitive processes are deeply rooted in bodies’ interactions with the world. Vocabulary learning is particularly relevant because many lexical meanings can be grounded in motor experiences, making it a compelling context for applying embodied cognition in education. Therefore, the present meta-analysis examines whether embodied instructional designs are effective in supporting vocabulary learning. Studies were identified through searches in databases (i.e., Web of Science, ERIC, PsycINFO, and Scopus), expert consultation, and backward reference in January 2026; ProQuest Dissertations & Theses Global was additionally searched in April 2026. Fifty-two studies met the inclusion criteria, and 442 effect sizes were included in the final analyses. A three-level meta-analytic model was employed, followed by moderator analyses to explore potential sources of heterogeneity. Results indicated that embodied learning significantly improved vocabulary learning outcomes compared with non-embodied conditions in both between-subject designs (Hedges’ g = 0.65) and within-subject designs (Hedges’ g = 0.27). However, publication bias was detected, indicating that the pooled effects may overestimate the true magnitude of the benefit. Moderator analyses indicated that movement-meaning congruency was the only moderator that was consistently observed across research designs, suggesting stronger effects when learners’ movements were aligned with the target word meanings. Overall, these findings emphasize the pedagogical potential of embodied learning for vocabulary learning and point to the need for future research to clarify how different forms of embodiment can support vocabulary learning.

items.title: Do you need to add (con)text to the equation? Subject-related, linguistic, and contextual factors in competence-oriented assessment
items.abstract: Background The growing emphasis on competence-oriented school assessments requires tests with more complex descriptions of real-life situations. However, few studies have systematically examined the associated changes in performance requirements, therefore, it is unclear how subject-specific and linguistic task characteristics (interacting) determine the level of difficulty of such tasks and the role of real-life context. Aims This study examines how linguistic, subject-related, and contextual task characteristics influence the empirical difficulty of reality-based assessment tasks. Sample The participants were 786 lower secondary school pupils from three comprehensive schools in a federal state in Germany. Methods In the experiment, three different language versions and three mathematical tasks were developed for 15 German-language factual texts and used in paper-and-pencil tests with a rotational design. Results The results of the generalized linear mixed models showed that mathematical and linguistic task factors significantly affect empirical task difficulty, although no interactions were found. The real-life context of the tasks proved to be relevant, as students' interest in respective contexts significantly influenced task success. Conclusions The findings highlight the need to differentiate specific linguistic features in task construction and acknowledge the previously neglected but critical role of real-life contexts in competence-oriented assessments.

items.title: From faux flipped to gamified flipped classrooms: scaffolding and cognitive load management
items.abstract: Background Students new to flipped classrooms frequently encounter challenges with motivation and comprehension when engaging with pre-class materials independently, particularly outside scheduled class hours. Aims This study examined a scaffolded flipped-learning approach that helped students move step by step from a Faux Flipped Classroom (FFC) to a Regular Flipped Classroom (RFC), and then to a Gamified Flipped Classroom (GFC) over one semester. The goal was to support students in adapting to flipped learning, managing their mental workload, and improving their learning performance. Method Mixed methods were employed in the data collection. For quantitative data, learning achievement was assessed with tests and self-rating scales measured cognitive load, while qualitative interviews provided more detailed feedback. Results The results revealed that students in the experimental group who learned through the scaffolding strategy performed better than their counterparts in the control group. Meanwhile, both groups demonstrated a small drop in intrinsic cognitive load, likely because they became more familiar with the tasks rather than because the material got easier. However, the scaffolded group showed a larger drop in unnecessary cognitive load and a larger increase in germane cognitive effort, suggesting the intervention helped students focus more on learning and less on confusion or figuring out what to do. Intrinsic and germane cognitive load should be interpreted cautiously because they are closely related. Conclusion This study contributes to Cognitive Load Theory and scaffolding research by showing that flipped classroom success depends not only on design but also on how students are gradually prepared to use it.

items.title: ICT use and student outcomes: Evidence from TIMSS 2019-2023
items.abstract: Background The integration of Information and Communication Technologies (ICT) in primary education has intensified over the last decade, yet empirical evidence on their association with academic performance and students' enjoyment of learning remains inconclusive. Aims This study investigates the association between the frequency of classroom ICT use and academic performance (Science and Mathematics) among Spanish fourth-grade students, examining whether this relationship differs between 2019 and 2023. A secondary aim explores the association with learning enjoyment. Sample We use Spanish fourth-grade student data from TIMSS 2019 and TIMSS 2023; the final estimation samples comprise 9252 (Mathematics) and 9216 (Science) students in 2019, and 4616 (Mathematics) and 6487 (Science) students in 2023. Methods We estimate linear regression models using plausible values, sampling weights, and Jackknife Repeated Replication (JRR). Learning enjoyment is modeled through ordinal logistic regression, and quantile regressions examine differential associations across the achievement distribution. Results In 2019, frequent ICT use was associated with lower academic performance, with numerically larger negative coefficients toward the lower end of the achievement distribution (differences across quantiles were not formally tested), and linked to higher Science enjoyment. Conversely, 2023 results show no significant association between ICT use and either outcome. Conclusions The results suggest that more frequent ICT use was not associated with improved academic performance, and was negatively associated with it in 2019. These patterns are consistent with, though do not directly test, the idea that device access alone may be insufficient without adequate pedagogical integration. These findings should be interpreted with caution, given the inherent methodological limitations of the study.

items.title: Explaining forgetting at different timescales requires a time-variant forgetting function
items.abstract: Employing memory models in practical applications provides an opportunity to test and refine theories on a large scale. The better models work in real-world scenarios, the more they can benefit educational practice. Using recall data spanning timescales from minutes to weeks, we find that a single forgetting curve cannot simultaneously capture short- and long-term performance, and show that an accurate model therefore requires a forgetting function that changes with time.

items.title: The effects of ICAP learning activities on learning outcomes
items.abstract: Background The Interactive-Constructive-Active-Passive (ICAP) framework makes assumptions about the relationships between observable types of learning activities (passive, active, constructive, interactive), cognitive processes, and learning outcomes. Yet, rigorous empirical studies are still lacking establishing the validity of the ICAP framework. Aims This study investigates the effects of student engagement in passive, active, constructive and interactive learning activities on their surface and deep knowledge gain, and their motivation. Additionally, the study aims to determine the associations between students’ cognitive processes, their learning activities, as well as surface and deep knowledge gain. Sample Participants were 249 pre-service teachers. Methods After reading a text on multimedia learning, participants were asked to reread the text (passive condition), to underline central information in the text (active condition), to work on three open-ended tasks addressing the text (constructive condition), or to work on the same tasks in pairs (interactive condition). Results No statistically significant effects of condition on surface or deep knowledge could be detected. Regarding motivation, participants in the interactive condition reported statistically significantly higher levels of perceived relatedness compared to all other conditions. Furthermore, only participants in the interactive condition reported statistically significantly higher levels of interactive cognitive processes compared to those in all other conditions. Constructive cognitive processes were statistically significantly negatively associated with deep knowledge gain. Conclusion The findings suggest that the empirical foundation supporting the ICAP framework may not yet be sufficiently robust. Yet, more research is needed that applies a more rigorous methodology exploring the ICAP framework.

items.title: Strict phonics instruction outperforms mixed phonics: Evidence from a large-scale study
items.abstract: Background Learning to read is a foundational milestone in formal education, and a large body of research supports the effectiveness of systematic phonics instruction in early literacy development. However, much less is known about whether different implementations of phonics instruction influence children’s reading outcomes. This study investigates whether variation within phonics-based instruction—specifically, strict versus mixed phonics approaches—is associated with differences in early reading development. Methods We combine survey data from more than 9000 first-grade teachers with longitudinal assessment data for over 139,000 pupils in France. Teachers were classified according to the instructional approaches they reported using and the characteristics of the reading materials employed in their classrooms. Pupils’ reading fluency and reading comprehension were measured using nationally administered standardized assessments conducted during Grade 1 and at the beginning of Grade 2. Results Multilevel analyses showed that pupils taught using strict phonics approaches achieved higher reading fluency and reading comprehension than those taught with mixed phonics approaches, with differences corresponding to approximately 0.11–0.16 standard deviations. These effects were substantially larger among pupils with weaker pre-reading skills and those attending socioeconomically disadvantaged schools. The findings remained robust across multiple complementary analyses designed to address potential selection effects and omitted-variable bias. Conclusion The findings demonstrate that meaningful differences in reading outcomes may arise not only from whether systematic phonics instruction is provided, but also from how it is implemented. They further suggest that optimizing the coherence of early phonics instruction may be particularly beneficial for pupils most at risk of reading difficulties.

items.title: Development of mental imagery strategy in a recall task as a function of word imageability and grade level in elementary school children
items.abstract: Objective This study investigated the development of mental imagery strategy in episodic memory as a function of word imageability and grade level in elementary school children. Method A total of 62 first-grade children, 61 third-grade children, and 60 fifth-grade children performed a free recall task involving high- and low-imageability words. A test of word memory was conducted using either a mental imagery strategy or a rehearsal strategy. Results The results showed that the benefit of the mental imagery strategy over the rehearsal condition was lower for first-graders than for third- or fifth-graders. Furthermore, word imageability influenced word recall to a greater extent in the mental imagery condition than in the rehearsal condition. Finally, the effect of word imageability did not interact with the children's age. Conclusion The findings are discussed in light of theories on the development of mental imagery and the cognitive processes underlying episodic memory.

items.title: Arithmetic development: a longitudinal observational study into the use of adaptive technology
items.abstract: Background AI-driven Adaptive learning technologies (ALTs) are widely used in primary education. These technologies have shown promising short-term results in arithmetic development. However, their long-term impact remains unclear. Aims This longitudinal observational study with a staggered introduction of the ALT investigated how the arithmetic ability of primary school students developed from grade 1 to grade 4 and how this development differed between students who used an ALT for arithmetic practice and those who did not. We also explored how individual and school characteristics moderated any developmental differences. Sample Data were collected over three years and included 7885 children, of whom 4603 (58.4%) used an ALT and 3282 (41.6%) did not. Method Multigroup SEM growth curve analyses compared arithmetic development across the ALT and control groups. Hierarchical models (linear and nonlinear) were tested, including time-invariant covariates (gender, socioeconomic status, prior arithmetic ability, and school size). Results Students who used the ALT showed a trend towards greater growth than those who did not, with small-to-medium effect sizes. Gender and individual SES differences were small in both conditions. Schools with a higher proportion of lower-SES students showed greater growth when using the ALT. The ALT also appeared to mitigate negative associations between school size and arithmetic development. Conclusions Use of the ALT was associated with numerically greater, though not statistically significant, arithmetic development in the long-term. Larger schools and schools with a higher percentage of lower SES students may consider using an ALT to support teachers in delivering tailored instruction.

items.title: Linking Language Attitudes to Proficiency Across Learning Contexts: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Correlational Evidence
items.abstract: Understanding the relationship between language attitudes and proficiency is essential for improving language proficiency and shaping effective educational and policy strategies. This correlational meta-analysis synthesizes 132 effect sizes nested within 46 independent samples from 33 research reports ( N = 20,505) to examine this relationship and how it is moderated by different attitude objects and contextual and methodological variables. The overall analysis revealed a significant small to medium association ( r = .34, 95% CI [.29, .39]), indicating that more favorable language attitudes tend to be linked to higher proficiency. Moderator analyses showed that the strength of this association varies depending on the specific object of the attitude (e.g., the language itself versus its speakers) and contextual factors such as language status. The analysis also highlights significant theoretical and methodological heterogeneity within existing research, calling for more holistic theoretical models, standardized assessment tools and more diverse sampling in future studies to enhance the certainty of evidence and inform educational practices.

items.title: Self-Directed Generative AI Use and Academic Development Among Secondary School Students: A Large-Scale, One-Year Longitudinal Study
items.abstract: Many students use generative AI (GenAI) tools for schoolwork on their own, without pedagogical guidance. Yet it remains unclear whether such use supports or undermines their academic development, or which students turn to it. We examined both questions using TOSCAneo data from 4,062 students in 136 secondary schools in Germany. Data were collected at the beginning and end of the 2023/2024 school year and included standardized achievement tests and measures of academic self-concept, value beliefs, and effort across six subjects. Students’ reported use of GenAI tools for academic activities formed two related factors: task-completion use and learning-oriented use. GenAI use increased over the school year for both task-completion use (d = 0.35) and learning-oriented use (d = 0.33), with only 5% of students never using GenAI. In cross-lagged panel models, lower prior achievement predicted more subsequent GenAI use in all six subjects for task-completion use and in five of six for learning-oriented use. Neither form of use predicted subsequent achievement. A use profile characterized by more task-completion and less learning-oriented use predicted lower subsequent effort in four of six subjects. No comparable pattern emerged for self-concept or value beliefs, and prior self-concept, value beliefs, and effort did not consistently predict later GenAI use. Overall, rather than predicting later achievement, self-directed GenAI use was related to which students turn to these tools and how much effort they invest. Guidance may therefore be particularly important for lower-achieving students, who use GenAI more than their higher-achieving peers.

items.title: Does Early Childhood Education and Care for Infants and Toddlers Cause Behavior Problems Up to Age 8?
items.abstract: Background: The causal effect of attending Early Childhood Education and Care (ECEC) for infants and toddlers on child behavior problems is contested. Yet, most previous research is correlational. Findings from previous research are mixed, but with some evidence of harmful effects on children’s behavior. Some correlational studies also suggest that ECEC may be most harmful for children from socioeconomically advantaged families. Methods: We estimate the effect of age of entry into ECEC on externalizing behavior problems at ages 3, 5, and 8 years in a large sample (n=66,394) from The Norwegian Mother, Father, and Child Cohort study (MoBa). We use two quasi-experimental methods, Two-Way Fixed-Effects models and Instrumental Variable models, that exploit variations in how early families enrolled their children in ECEC due to a national scale-up of publicly funded centers. Results: In this high-powered, rigorous approach to testing the causal impact of age of entry into ECEC, we find no evidence that entry around age 1 relative to later affects behavior problems either during preschool years (at ages 3 or 5) or after school entry (at age 8 years). We also find no evidence that these effects vary by parental education or family income. Conclusion: We find no evidence suggesting that early entry into ECEC has harmful consequences for children’s behavior regulation, during the preschool years or after school entry. We argue that our null results may be due to ECEC pedagogy in Norway that emphasizes young children’s well-being and playful learning experiences.
